title: What’s next for UK tourism: cost, coastal towns, staff and strategy
label: 13 October 2026 · Tourism inquiry (oral evidence)
summary: Two panels of travel writers, creators and tourism operators told MPs that British holiday habits have changed: people are taking shorter, cheaper trips, favouring short‑term rentals and experiences pushed by social media, while coastal towns struggle with cost, sewage, seasonality and weak marketing. Witnesses called for clearer government strategy, practical support for workforce training, better local transport and targeted marketing of UK destinations — and identified specific fixes such as changing weather icons, reforming gift‑aid rules for attractions and careful use of any visitor levy.

chapters.title: How holiday habits have shifted
chapters.takeaway: British holidays are shorter and cheaper, driven by cost pressures, growth of short‑term rentals and demand for shareable experiences.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do tourists' expectations and priorities in the UK look different than before?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Yes. Average holiday length has fallen from a 14‑night model decades ago to about 9.6 days overall, and even short breaks have shortened—3.3 days down to 2.9 in some cases.

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: People are 'trading down': either shorter stays or cheaper places. Since 2021 expenditure and duration have fallen and many guests now choose STRs—Airbnb‑type lets—now about 20–25% of the market while hotels are 40–45%.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Families now look for new experiences they can share on social media—activities, cool cafes, child‑friendly things—not just lying on a beach.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Cost matters: people self‑cater more, use travel‑hack tips to save, and try to spend on experiences rather than pricey hotel extras.

chapters.title: Coastal towns, the visitor experience and environmental worries
chapters.takeaway: Seaside towns face falling overnight stays, high costs, seasonal pressure and growing public concern about water quality.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are UK coastal destinations adapting to these changes?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Not really. Overnight stays at the British seaside have dropped 18% in ten years. Many resorts were built for a short Victorian season and need money to maintain big buildings and services—money they don't have.

turns.speaker: Mr Bayo Alaba
turns.text: What practical things can towns like Southend do to attract more visitors?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Two models work: (1) external investment and grant capture, like Great Yarmouth using renewables income and heritage grants; (2) community‑led renewal, like Bude, with local engagement and initiatives such as beach cleans and a 'coastal parliament'.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Events pull people in—music, food festivals, weekend activations make places feel alive and bring return visits.

turns.speaker: Dr Rupa Huq
turns.text: Are the seaside towns still viable as conference or event venues?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Large conferences now go to cities because they can handle big crowds, security and accommodation in one place; many coastal towns lack the capacity.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: A major issue is sewage in bathing water. People see app alerts and toilet paper on beaches; it puts them off visiting the coast.

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: BEACH ratings are often historic; what matters are CSO discharges that can happen anytime. People rely on third‑party apps (Surfers Against Sewage etc.) to know real‑time water quality — that harms confidence in the British coast.

chapters.title: Pricing, levies and how to manage visitor numbers
chapters.takeaway: High UK prices make many people prefer cheap, all‑inclusive holidays abroad; visitor levies must be designed carefully if used.

turns.speaker: Mr Bayo Alaba
turns.text: Why do many UK residents go abroad rather than holiday at home?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Value for money is the main driver. A mid‑range Cornwall hotel break can be far more expensive than an all‑inclusive Spanish week, even after adding food costs.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: School holiday pricing spikes make domestic breaks prohibitively expensive for many families.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: What about an overnight visitor levy to manage overtourism and raise funds?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Small charges, like £5, won't deter tourists; they'd need to be significant to change behaviour, but that risks pushing visitors elsewhere. Another option is to develop UK as a lower‑volume, higher‑spend destination.

turns.speaker: Alex Polizzi
turns.text: I'm against levies for places like Cornwall because domestic visitors are often lower‑income; extra charges could deter them and harm local small businesses.

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: We're pragmatic: an overnight levy could be useful if locally led, simple to administer and ring‑fenced for tourism, but we recognise local opposition.

chapters.title: Workforce, regulation and practical fixes
chapters.takeaway: Tourism and attractions need help with rising costs, staff recruitment, training and clearer government backing; some specific, implementable fixes were suggested.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What is the health of the sector and what would make the biggest difference?

turns.speaker: Alex Polizzi
turns.text: Costs have shot up: business rates, utilities, NI and minimum wage increases added nearly £950,000 to my three hotels' costs since Feb 2024. Staff costs can be nearly half of turnover.

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: At Chester Zoo we employ 1,200 people. The national insurance rise cost us £600,000 overnight. We need public support; local funding for destination marketing has fallen to near zero in many areas.

turns.speaker: Mr Bayo Alaba
turns.text: What blocks recruiting and keeping staff?

turns.speaker: Alex Polizzi
turns.text: Transport in rural areas is poor; staff need cars or family taxis. Housing and staff accommodation are expensive; allowances staff can keep are small; and parental perceptions make hospitality a 'last choice' career.

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: We run apprenticeships and many staff stay, but chefs and night‑shift roles are hard to fill. Training is largely funded by employers; Government training support is limited.

turns.speaker: Dr Rupa Huq
turns.text: Should the industry have a stronger single voice in Government?

turns.speaker: Alex Polizzi
turns.text: Yes. We lack a properly funded, professional centre of excellence for hospitality training and a visible ministerial champion who understands the sector's realities.

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: Zoos also fall between Departments: DEFRA regulates animals, but we are tourism, education and science. We'd like clearer departmental ownership so funds and policy fit our mixed role.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: Any simple tech or digital fixes that would help attractions?

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: Yes — weather apps. Many visitors check a single weather icon and change plans. If major apps showed several icons across the day (morning, lunch, afternoon, evening) it would reduce lost visits — we estimate a bad icon day can cost us six figures.

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Also: better, visible domestic promotion. Spain’s tourist board successfully promoted regions to Spaniards; the UK needs stronger, consistent campaigns so people remember what’s on their doorstep.

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: And a change to gift‑aid rules: currently attractions can only claim if a visitor donates at least 10% on top of a ticket; removing that threshold could unlock about £1m a year for our zoo.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Finally, real‑time clarity on sewer discharges and stricter action on bathing water would restore public confidence in the coast.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you each could ask Government for one change over five years, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: Put zoos and similar attractions into a single, coherent government framework so policy, funding and regulation match what we actually do (conservation, education, tourism).

turns.speaker: Alex Polizzi
turns.text: Create and back a professional centre of excellence for hospitality to professionalise training, reassure parents and provide a recognised career pathway.

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Invest in stronger domestic marketing, and tackle bathing water quality to stop the reputation damage that's driving people away from the coast.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Make domestic holidays affordable for families—school‑term pricing spikes and the ability to get a decent, affordable family break matter hugely.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all — practical suggestions, clear problem areas and specific asks for Government to consider.
